title: Observability Across Services
summary: Observability is how you understand a distributed Go system from the outside using its outputs. It rests on **three pillars** — metrics (aggregate numbers), logs (discrete events), and traces (the path of one request across services). The glue is a **trace/correlation ID** that flows through `context.Context` and every log line, so you can pivot from a slow metric to the exact trace to the exact log. Master OpenTelemetry spans, context propagation across HTTP/gRPC, structured logging with slog, and the RED/USE methods, and you can debug a request across N services instead of guessing.

subtopics.title: The three pillars: metrics, logs, traces
subtopics.explanation: Metrics are cheap aggregate time series (request rate, error rate, p99 latency) great for alerting; logs are discrete, high-cardinality events good for detail; traces stitch together the causal path of a single request across services. Each answers a different question — 'is something wrong?' (metrics), 'what exactly happened?' (logs), 'where in the call graph?' (traces). For observability across services, you need all three wired to a shared trace ID so you can pivot between them instead of treating them as three disconnected tools.

subtopics.title: Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry
subtopics.explanation: A trace is a tree of spans; each span records an operation with a start/end time, attributes, and a parent link. OpenTelemetry gives you a vendor-neutral API to create spans and export them to backends like Jaeger or Tempo via OTLP. You create a child span at each meaningful boundary (handler, DB call, RPC) so the backend can render the request as a waterfall. Distributed tracing is the pillar that makes cross-service observability possible — it is the only view that shows the whole request as one connected story.

subtopics.title: Trace context propagation
subtopics.explanation: A trace only stays connected if the trace context (trace ID + span ID) travels with the request across process boundaries. OTel serializes it into carriers — the W3C `traceparent` HTTP header, or gRPC metadata — via a propagator; the receiving service extracts it and continues the trace. In Go you rarely do this by hand: `otelhttp` and the gRPC OTel interceptors inject on the client and extract on the server automatically. Propagation is what turns N independent per-service traces into one distributed trace, so it is the linchpin of observability across services.

subtopics.title: Correlation/trace IDs in every log line
subtopics.explanation: The magic of observability is being able to jump from a metric spike to a trace to the logs for that exact request. That only works if every log line carries the trace ID. You pull the active SpanContext out of the request's context.Context and add trace_id (and span_id) as structured fields on the logger, so a single grep or Loki query returns every log across every service for one request. Threading the trace ID through context into logs is what unifies the pillars — it is the correlation key that ties cross-service observability together.

subtopics.title: Structured logging at scale (slog/zap)
subtopics.explanation: At fleet scale, human-readable log strings are useless; you emit structured key/value logs (JSON) so a log platform can index and query them. Go's standard slog (or zap for performance) produces structured records, and you attach request-scoped fields — trace ID, user ID, route — once via logger.With so every downstream line carries them without repetition. Structured, request-scoped logging is the observability pillar that gives you queryable detail across services, and pairing it with the trace ID makes each line pivotable to a trace.

subtopics.title: RED/USE methods & SLOs
subtopics.explanation: The RED method describes a service by three metrics — Rate (requests/sec), Errors (failed/sec), and Duration (latency distribution); the USE method describes a resource by Utilization, Saturation, and Errors. RED is for request-driven services, USE for machines/queues. You turn these into SLIs (measured indicators) and SLOs (targets, e.g. 99.9% of requests under 300ms), and alert on error budget burn. The RED/USE methods give observability across services a consistent measurement vocabulary, so every service's health is described the same way and rolls up into meaningful SLOs.

foundations.overview: Observability across services is the ability to answer new questions about a running distributed system without shipping new code, using the three pillars — metrics, logs, and traces. The key insight is that these pillars are only powerful when correlated: a trace ID generated at the edge flows through context.Context, rides across every HTTP/gRPC hop via OpenTelemetry propagation, and lands on every log line and span. Once that correlation exists, you can debug a request across N services by pivoting from a metric to a trace to the logs, instead of tailing logs on each box.
foundations.formalDefinition: Observability is a property of a system: the degree to which its internal state can be inferred from its external outputs (metrics, logs, traces). A trace is a directed tree of spans sharing a trace ID; a span is a timed operation with attributes and a parent. Propagation is the serialization of trace context into a carrier (W3C traceparent header, gRPC metadata) so a downstream service can continue the same trace.
foundations.whyItMatters: In a monolith you can attach a debugger; in a fleet of services a single user request fans out across many processes, and without correlated telemetry an incident becomes hours of guessing. Distributed tracing and trace-ID-tagged structured logs turn 'which of the 12 services is slow?' into a single trace lookup. It is also a staple of senior backend and SRE interviews.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a trace as a package's shipment tracking. The trace ID is the tracking number; each span is a scan event ('arrived at facility', 'out for delivery') with a timestamp and location. Propagation is stamping the same tracking number onto the package at every handoff between carriers, so the whole journey shows up under one number no matter how many companies touched it.
foundations.runtimePerspective: At runtime, otelhttp/gRPC interceptors extract trace context from the incoming carrier and store the SpanContext in r.Context(); your tracer.Start reads that context to attach child spans to the right parent. Spans are buffered by a BatchSpanProcessor and exported asynchronously over OTLP to Jaeger/Tempo, so tracing adds little request-path latency. slog reads the same context to stamp trace_id onto each record. Metrics are updated in-memory and scraped/pushed on an interval.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Request tracing across an API gateway plus downstream microservices, latency waterfalls to find the slow hop, error-rate and p99 dashboards per route (RED), resource dashboards for queues and hosts (USE), and SLO/error-budget alerting. Every serious Go microservice fleet runs OpenTelemetry with a collector exporting to Jaeger/Tempo, Prometheus, and a log store.
foundations.businessImpact: Correlated observability collapses mean-time-to-resolution during outages, directly protecting revenue and SLAs. SLOs and error budgets let the business make explicit reliability-vs-velocity tradeoffs instead of reacting to every alert, and good tracing reduces the on-call toil that burns out engineering teams.
foundations.engineeringImpact: A shared telemetry contract (OTel + a trace ID in every log) means any engineer can debug any service with the same tools, and instrumentation lives in middleware/interceptors instead of being sprinkled through business logic. This keeps handlers clean and makes new services observable by default.
foundations.performanceImpact: Tracing overhead is small when spans are batched and sampling is applied; the real cost is unsampled high-throughput tracing and synchronous exporters, which add latency and memory. Structured JSON logging is heavier than plain text but far cheaper than the incident it prevents; hot-path logging should be leveled and sampled. Metrics are the cheapest pillar and the right place to alert.
commonUseCases: Distributed tracing across an API gateway and downstream services with OpenTelemetry
Trace-ID-correlated structured logs (slog/zap) queried across the fleet
RED dashboards (rate/errors/p99) per route and USE dashboards per resource
SLO/error-budget alerting on latency and error rate

commonMisconceptions.myth: Logs alone are enough to debug distributed systems.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Logs are per-service and discrete; without a trace ID correlating them and a trace showing the call graph, you can't see which hop was slow or how the request flowed across services.

It's automatic only where you use instrumented transports (otelhttp, gRPC OTel interceptors). Custom clients, message queues, and new goroutines require you to inject/extract or pass the context yourself, or the trace breaks.
Unsampled traces and debug logs on hot paths cost latency, money, and cognitive load. You sample traces, level and sample logs, and rely on cheap metrics for alerting.

commonMisconceptions.myth: An SLO is just an uptime percentage.
commonMisconceptions.reality: An SLO is a target on a specific SLI (e.g. p99 latency or success rate) over a window, with an error budget that governs how much unreliability is acceptable — not a vague '99.9% up' claim.

interactiveExamples.title: Server span + child spans + trace-ID logging in one handler
interactiveExamples.explanation: otelhttp.NewHandler starts a server span from the incoming traceparent. Inside, tracer.Start creates a child span for the DB step, and loggerFrom stamps the active trace ID onto every log line so the log and the trace share a correlation key.

code.caption: The server span (otelhttp), a child span (tracer.Start), and a trace-ID-tagged slog line all share one trace context.

interactiveExamples.title: Propagating trace context to a downstream service over HTTP
interactiveExamples.explanation: The gateway span calls a downstream service. otelhttp.NewTransport injects the traceparent header from ctx so the downstream continues the SAME trace. Without passing the request's context, the header is never injected and the trace splits in two.

code.caption: otelhttp.NewTransport + NewRequestWithContext(ctx, ...) inject the traceparent, so the inventory service continues the same distributed trace.
code.expectedOutput:
// Outbound header: traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
// One trace in Jaeger: gateway -> callInventory -> inventory-service

interactiveExamples.title: RED metrics middleware with a status-capturing writer
interactiveExamples.explanation: This middleware records Rate, Errors, and Duration from one histogram labeled by route, method, and status. It wraps the ResponseWriter to capture the status code (which the interface doesn't expose) so error rate can be derived from status>=500.

code.caption: A single labeled histogram yields the RED signals: total count is Rate, the status label yields Errors, and the buckets yield Duration/p99 for SLOs.

checkpoints.prompt: Which pillar of observability answers 'where in the cross-service call graph did this single request spend its time?'
checkpoints.explanation: Traces stitch a single request's spans across services into a waterfall, showing exactly which hop was slow. Metrics tell you something is wrong in aggregate; logs give per-service detail; only traces show the causal path of one request across N services.

checkpoints.prompt: This downstream call is supposed to continue the caller's trace but always starts a brand-new, disconnected trace. What's the root issue?
options: The request has no context, so there's no trace context to inject
You must set the traceparent header manually
checkpoints.explanation: otelhttp.NewTransport injects the traceparent from the request's context, but http.NewRequest gives a request with context.Background() — no active span. Use http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, ...) so the current span is in scope and the transport can inject it; otherwise the downstream starts a fresh, orphaned trace.

checkpoints.prompt: Extract the active trace ID from the request context to tag the logger.
checkpoints.explanation: SpanContextFromContext returns the active SpanContext; sc.TraceID().String() is the canonical trace ID that ties this log line to the trace and to logs in other services. A fresh uuid wouldn't correlate, and the raw traceparent header is the on-the-wire form, not the parsed ID.

checkpoints.prompt: A RED histogram is labeled by status. A handler returns 500 for one request and 200 for another. What can you compute from this one metric?
options: Rate, error rate (status>=500), and the latency distribution (p99)
checkpoints.explanation: A labeled histogram carries all three RED signals: the total observation count is Rate, filtering the status label to >=500 gives Errors, and the bucket counts give the Duration distribution for p99 and latency SLOs. One well-labeled histogram replaces three separate metrics.

codeLab.title: A slog.Handler that auto-injects the trace ID
codeLab.instructions: Implement `TraceHandler` wrapping an inner slog.Handler so that every record automatically gets a `trace_id` attribute pulled from the context's SpanContext (when one is present). Implement the `Handle(ctx, record)` method: if `trace.SpanContextFromContext(ctx)` has a trace ID, add `slog.String("trace_id", id)` to the record before delegating to the inner handler. If there's no trace ID, delegate unchanged.
hints: Embed slog.Handler so Enabled/WithAttrs/WithGroup are promoted and you only override Handle.
Use trace.SpanContextFromContext(ctx) and guard on sc.HasTraceID() before adding attributes.
slog.Record has AddAttrs — call it to append trace_id, then delegate with h.Handler.Handle(ctx, r).

codeLab.title: Build RED-metrics middleware with a status recorder
codeLab.instructions: Implement `REDMetrics(reqDur *prometheus.HistogramVec) func(http.Handler) http.Handler`. It must wrap the ResponseWriter to capture the status code (default 200), call next, then Observe the elapsed seconds into `reqDur` labeled by route (`r.Pattern`), method, and the captured status. This one Observe must yield all three RED signals.
hints: Return func(next http.Handler) http.Handler because the middleware is configured with the histogram.
Embed http.ResponseWriter in a recorder and override WriteHeader to save the status (default 200 for handlers that only Write).
Label the Observe with r.Pattern (route), r.Method, and strconv.Itoa(status) so one histogram gives Rate, Errors, and Duration.

debuggingLab.title: Background spans are orphaned: the trace splits across a goroutine
debuggingLab.symptom: In Jaeger the main request trace looks complete, but the work done in a background goroutine (a cache warm / audit write) appears as a separate, single-span trace with no parent. The trace ID differs from the request's, so you can't see the background work in the request's waterfall.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: tracer.Start attaches the new span as a child of whatever span is in the context you pass it. The goroutine starts its span from context.Background(), which has no active SpanContext, so OTel begins a brand-new trace with a fresh trace ID. The background span therefore can't be linked to the request's trace and shows up orphaned. The request context DOES hold the parent span — it just wasn't passed into the goroutine.
commonMistakes: Passing context.Background() (or context.TODO()) into a goroutine instead of the request context.
Capturing r.Context() directly in a goroutine that may outlive the request, so the span is cancelled when the handler returns.
Forgetting that spawning a goroutine is a boundary just like an RPC — trace context must be carried across it explicitly.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Propagate the parent span into the goroutine without tying its lifetime to the request. Derive a detached-but-linked context from the request's context so the background span becomes a child of the request's trace but isn't cancelled when the handler returns.

solution.expectedOutput:
// One trace in Jaeger: server span -> {respond, auditWrite}
// auditWrite now shares the request's trace_id instead of starting a new trace

theory.question: Explain the three pillars of observability and why correlating them with a trace ID matters in a Go microservice fleet.
theory.directAnswer: The three pillars are metrics (cheap aggregate time series for alerting — rate, errors, p99), logs (discrete high-cardinality events for detail), and traces (the causal path of one request across services as a tree of spans). Individually each answers a different question, but their power comes from correlation: a trace ID generated at the edge flows through context.Context, propagates across every HTTP/gRPC hop, and is stamped onto every span and every log line. That shared key lets you pivot from a latency-metric spike to the exact slow trace to the exact logs for that request across all services, instead of tailing logs on each box.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Metrics, logs, and traces, unified by a trace/correlation ID that travels in context.Context.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A single request fans out across many processes; no one pillar shows the whole picture, so you correlate them.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: OTel propagation carries the trace ID across boundaries; slog reads the SpanContext to tag logs; metrics are labeled per route.

theory.whyImportant: It is the difference between a minutes-long trace lookup and an hours-long guessing game during an incident, and it's a core senior backend/SRE interview topic.
theory.realWorldExample: A p99 alert on the checkout route leads you to a slow trace whose waterfall shows the inventory hop is slow; the inventory logs for that same trace_id reveal a lock contention error.

followUps.question: Which pillar do you alert on and why?
followUps.answer: Metrics — they're cheap, low-cardinality, and stable, so they make good SLO alerts; you then drill into traces and logs for the cause.

followUps.question: Why not just put everything in logs?
followUps.answer: Logs are per-service and expensive at high cardinality; they can't cheaply express aggregate rates or show the cross-service call graph the way metrics and traces do.

theory.question: How does trace context propagation work in Go with OpenTelemetry across HTTP and gRPC boundaries?
theory.directAnswer: Trace context (trace ID + span ID + flags) is stored in context.Context as a SpanContext. To cross a process boundary, OTel serializes it into a carrier using a propagator: for HTTP the W3C TraceContext propagator writes a 'traceparent' header; for gRPC the OTel interceptors write it into request metadata. On the client you use an instrumented transport (otelhttp.NewTransport) or gRPC stats handler/interceptor that injects the header from ctx; on the server otelhttp.NewHandler or the gRPC server interceptor extracts it and starts a server span as a child of the caller's span. The two critical requirements are setting a global propagator (otel.SetTextMapPropagator) and always passing the request's context (e.g. http.NewRequestWithContext) so there's a span to inject.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Serialization of SpanContext into a carrier (traceparent header / gRPC metadata) so a downstream service continues the same trace.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: context.Context doesn't cross process boundaries; the trace ID must be encoded on the wire and re-hydrated.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A propagator injects on the client from ctx and extracts on the server into ctx; instrumented transports/interceptors do this automatically.

theory.whyImportant: Broken propagation is the number-one reason distributed traces come out fragmented, and knowing exactly where it happens is a common interview probe.
theory.realWorldExample: A gateway calls two downstream services with otelhttp.NewTransport; both continue the gateway's trace, so Jaeger shows one waterfall spanning all three services.

followUps.question: What breaks propagation across a message queue?
followUps.answer: Queues aren't HTTP/gRPC, so you must manually inject the trace context into message headers on publish and extract it on consume using propagator.Inject/Extract with a custom carrier.

followUps.question: Why set otel.SetTextMapPropagator explicitly?
followUps.answer: The default OTel propagator is a no-op; without setting TraceContext (and optionally Baggage) nothing is injected or extracted and every hop starts a new trace.

theory.question: Contrast the RED and USE methods and explain how they turn into SLIs and SLOs.
theory.directAnswer: RED describes a request-driven service by three signals — Rate (requests/sec), Errors (failed requests/sec), and Duration (latency distribution). USE describes a resource (CPU, disk, queue) by Utilization, Saturation, and Errors. RED is what you put on a service dashboard; USE is what you put on an infrastructure dashboard, and they complement each other (RED tells you the service is slow, USE tells you the disk is saturated). You pick SLIs — measurable indicators like success rate or p99 latency — set SLOs as targets over a window (e.g. 99.9% of requests succeed and 99% are under 300ms over 30 days), and derive an error budget (0.1% may fail); you then alert on burn rate of that budget rather than on every blip.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two complementary measurement frameworks: RED for services, USE for resources, feeding SLIs/SLOs.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To give every service and resource a consistent, minimal set of health signals and a principled way to alert.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: RED comes from a labeled request histogram; USE from resource gauges; SLOs are targets on chosen SLIs with an error budget.

theory.whyImportant: SLIs/SLOs let teams trade reliability against velocity explicitly and avoid alert fatigue, which is central to SRE and senior backend interviews.
theory.realWorldExample: A checkout service tracks RED via one Prometheus histogram; its SLO is 99.9% success and p99 < 300ms; when the 1h+6h burn-rate alert fires, on-call knows the error budget is at risk.

followUps.question: When is RED not enough?
followUps.answer: For non-request workloads (batch jobs, queues, caches) USE is more informative; you often need both — RED for the API, USE for the datastore behind it.

followUps.question: Why alert on error-budget burn rate instead of raw error rate?
followUps.answer: Burn-rate alerting ties severity to how fast you're consuming the budget, catching fast burns quickly while ignoring tiny, budget-safe blips, which reduces false pages.

scenario.question: A user reports checkout is slow, but each of your six services looks healthy on its own dashboard. How do you use observability to find the slow hop across the fleet?
scenario.directAnswer: Start from the correlation key. Get a trace ID for a slow checkout — either from the response header, the frontend, or by filtering the checkout RED histogram for high-latency requests and grabbing an exemplar trace ID. Open that trace in Jaeger/Tempo and read the waterfall: it shows every span across all six services with per-span durations, so the slow hop is the widest bar (say, a 900ms DB span in the inventory service). Then jump from that span's trace_id to the inventory logs filtered by the same trace_id to see the exact error or slow query. Confirm it's systemic (not a one-off) by checking that service's RED Duration/p99 and USE saturation for its datastore. This works because the trace ID threads metrics, traces, and logs together.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A cross-service debugging workflow that pivots metric -> trace -> logs via a shared trace ID.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Per-service dashboards hide problems that only appear in the interaction between services on one request.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A trace waterfall localizes the slow span; the trace_id filters logs to that request; RED/USE confirm scope.

scenario.whyImportant: This is the everyday value of observability and a very common 'walk me through debugging' interview scenario.
scenario.realWorldExample: The checkout trace shows the inventory span at 900ms; inventory logs for that trace_id show 'lock wait timeout'; USE on the inventory DB shows connection-pool saturation, pinpointing the root cause.

followUps.question: What if the slow request isn't sampled and has no trace?
followUps.answer: Use tail-based sampling or exemplars so slow/error requests are always kept, or temporarily raise the sampling rate; otherwise you may miss the exact slow trace.

followUps.question: How would you make the trace ID easy to grab for support tickets?
followUps.answer: Return it in a response header (e.g. X-Trace-Id) and surface it in the UI/error page so users and support can quote it directly.

scenario.question: After adding a background goroutine that emits its own spans, your traces are fragmenting: the background work shows up as separate single-span traces. What's happening and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: tracer.Start attaches the new span as a child of whatever span is in the context you pass it. If the goroutine calls tracer.Start(context.Background(), ...) there's no active SpanContext, so OTel starts a brand-new trace with its own trace ID — hence the orphaned single-span traces. You must carry the request's trace context into the goroutine. But you can't just capture r.Context() directly if the goroutine outlives the request, because that context is cancelled when the handler returns. The fix is context.WithoutCancel(r.Context()) (Go 1.21+): it preserves the trace context (and other values) while dropping the request's cancellation, so the background span becomes a child of the request's trace and survives the handler returning. For work that shouldn't share the request's fate at all, use span links instead of parent-child.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A trace-continuity fix for spans created in goroutines that outlive the request.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A goroutine is a boundary like an RPC — trace context must be carried across it, and lifetime must be managed.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: context.WithoutCancel keeps the parent SpanContext but detaches cancellation, so the background span joins the request's trace.

scenario.whyImportant: Orphaned spans from goroutines are a classic, subtle instrumentation bug that shows up constantly in real Go services.
scenario.realWorldExample: An audit-write goroutine started from context.Background() produced thousands of one-span traces until switched to context.WithoutCancel(r.Context()), after which audit spans appeared under each request's trace.

followUps.question: When would you use a span link instead of a child span?
followUps.answer: When the background work is causally related but logically independent (e.g. batched async processing), a link records the relationship without making it a child of a single request's span.

followUps.question: Why not just pass r.Context() straight into the goroutine?
followUps.answer: r.Context() is cancelled when the handler returns, so the goroutine's work (and its span) would be cut short; WithoutCancel keeps the values but removes that cancellation.

systemDesign.question: Design an observability stack for a fleet of Go microservices so any engineer can debug any request end-to-end. Walk through the components and data flow.
systemDesign.directAnswer: Instrument every service with OpenTelemetry: wrap inbound HTTP with otelhttp.NewHandler and gRPC with the OTel server interceptor to start server spans, and wrap outbound calls with otelhttp.NewTransport / client interceptors to propagate trace context via W3C traceparent. Set a global TraceContext propagator. Create child spans at meaningful boundaries (DB, RPC, cache) with attributes. Emit structured JSON logs via slog through a custom handler that stamps trace_id/span_id from the context onto every line. Expose RED metrics from one labeled request histogram (route/method/status) plus USE metrics for resources, scraped by Prometheus. Send spans over OTLP to a collector, which fans out to Jaeger/Tempo (traces), Prometheus (metrics), and a log store (Loki/ELK). Apply sampling (head-based at the edge, ideally tail-based at the collector so errors/slow requests are always kept). Define SLIs/SLOs per service with error-budget burn-rate alerts. The unifying design choice is the trace ID present in traces, metrics exemplars, and every log line so engineers pivot freely across all three.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An end-to-end OTel-based telemetry pipeline: instrumentation, collector, backends, and correlation via trace ID.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A fleet needs a uniform telemetry contract so any request is debuggable across service boundaries by any engineer.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Interceptors propagate context and emit spans; slog tags logs with trace_id; a collector routes traces/metrics/logs to their backends.

systemDesign.whyImportant: It demonstrates you can operate, not just build, distributed systems — a core senior/staff and SRE interview expectation.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: This is essentially how large Go shops run OTel with a collector exporting to Tempo, Prometheus, and Loki, with trace_id linking Grafana panels across all three.

followUps.question: Head-based vs tail-based sampling — which and why?
followUps.answer: Head-based (decide at the edge) is cheap but may drop the rare error/slow trace; tail-based at the collector keeps all traces long enough to sample errors/high latency, at higher collector cost.

followUps.question: How do you keep instrumentation out of business logic?
followUps.answer: Put propagation and span creation in middleware/interceptors and wrap clients (otelhttp, DB drivers), so handlers stay clean and services are observable by default.

followUps.question: How do you control telemetry cost at scale?
followUps.answer: Sample traces, level and sample high-volume logs, keep metric cardinality bounded (avoid unbounded label values like user IDs), and set retention per backend.

systemDesign.question: Design an SLO and alerting system for a critical Go API so on-call gets paged on real problems, not noise. What SLIs, SLOs, and alerts do you choose?
systemDesign.directAnswer: Pick SLIs that reflect user experience: request success rate (non-5xx / total) and latency (fraction of requests under a threshold, e.g. p99 < 300ms), both derived from the RED request histogram. Set SLOs as targets over a rolling window: 99.9% availability and 99% of requests under 300ms over 30 days. That defines an error budget (0.1% of requests may fail per month). Instead of alerting on instantaneous error rate, alert on error-budget burn rate using multi-window multi-burn-rate rules: a fast-burn alert (e.g. 2% of the budget in 1h, confirmed over 5m) pages immediately, while a slow-burn alert (10% over 6h) files a ticket. Add USE-based alerts for saturation of underlying resources as leading indicators. This keeps paging tied to user-visible harm and to how fast reliability is degrading, drastically cutting false pages.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An SLI/SLO/error-budget framework with multi-window burn-rate alerting.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Alerting on raw thresholds causes fatigue; SLO burn-rate alerting ties pages to user impact and urgency.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: SLIs come from the RED histogram; SLOs set targets and an error budget; burn-rate rules over multiple windows decide page vs ticket.

systemDesign.whyImportant: Well-designed SLOs and burn-rate alerts are the modern SRE standard and a frequent system-design interview theme.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: A payments API pages only when a 1h/5m fast-burn rule shows the 30-day error budget draining quickly, so a brief blip during a deploy doesn't wake anyone.

followUps.question: Why multi-window multi-burn-rate instead of a single threshold?
followUps.answer: It catches fast catastrophic burns quickly (short window) while requiring a longer window to confirm, reducing both missed incidents and false pages.

followUps.question: What happens when the error budget is exhausted?
followUps.answer: Teams typically freeze risky feature releases and prioritize reliability work until the budget recovers, making the reliability/velocity tradeoff explicit.

coding.question: Implement a helper `LogWithTrace(ctx context.Context, base *slog.Logger) *slog.Logger` that returns a logger tagged with the active trace_id and span_id when a span is present in the context, and returns the base logger unchanged otherwise.
coding.thoughtProcess: The trace context lives in context.Context as a SpanContext, retrieved with trace.SpanContextFromContext. If it has a valid trace ID, derive a child logger via base.With adding trace_id and span_id as string fields; the derived logger inherits these on every subsequent line. If there's no active span (e.g. a background job with no trace), return base unchanged so we don't emit empty correlation fields. Keep it allocation-light by only calling With when a span exists.
coding.lineByLine: SpanContextFromContext extracts the SpanContext OTel stored in ctx. HasTraceID guards the case where no span is active, so we don't attach empty fields — we just return base. When a span exists, base.With returns a new *slog.Logger that carries trace_id and span_id (as canonical hex strings) on every record, so all downstream logs are correlated to the trace without repeating the fields.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) — a context lookup and, when a span exists, one logger clone.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) — one derived logger when a span is present; none otherwise.

followUps.question: Why guard on HasTraceID instead of always calling With?
followUps.answer: Without an active span, TraceID/SpanID are all-zero; attaching them adds noise and misleading correlation fields, so returning base is cleaner and cheaper.

followUps.question: How would you make every log line trace-tagged without calling this helper each time?
followUps.answer: Wrap the slog.Handler so its Handle method reads the context's SpanContext and injects trace_id automatically, then use InfoContext/ErrorContext so the context reaches the handler.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Instrument at the edges: otelhttp/gRPC interceptors start server spans and propagate context; wrapped clients continue traces to downstream services. Keep span creation and propagation in middleware/interceptors and instrumented drivers so business handlers stay clean. Emit structured logs via an slog handler that stamps trace_id from context. Expose RED metrics from one labeled histogram and USE metrics for resources. Ship everything through an OpenTelemetry Collector that fans out to Jaeger/Tempo, Prometheus, and a log store, so backends are swappable behind OTLP.
productionDeepDive.performance: Batch spans with a BatchSpanProcessor and export asynchronously over OTLP so tracing barely touches the request path. Apply sampling (head-based at the edge, tail-based at the collector to always keep errors/slow traces) to control volume. Structured JSON logging is heavier than plain text — level it, sample hot-path logs, and avoid logging in tight loops. Metrics are the cheapest pillar; keep cardinality bounded and prefer histograms for latency SLOs.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Trace context lives in context.Context, so every goroutine that does traced work must receive that context; spawning a goroutine is a boundary like an RPC. For background work that outlives a request use context.WithoutCancel to keep the trace context while dropping cancellation, or use span links for logically independent async work. Exporters and metric registries are safe for concurrent use, but never share a single span across goroutines without care — end it once.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Always flush spans on shutdown (tp.Shutdown with a deadline) so in-flight telemetry isn't lost on deploy. Telemetry must never take down the service: use non-blocking exporters, drop on backpressure, and make the collector a soft dependency. Record errors on spans (span.RecordError + SetStatus) so failures are visible in traces. Tie alerting to SLO error-budget burn rather than raw thresholds to page on real degradation.
productionDeepDive.observability: This topic IS observability: three correlated pillars. In practice, every log line carries trace_id/span_id, every service exposes RED metrics and /metrics, and traces span the whole request via propagation. Use exemplars to jump from a latency histogram bucket straight to a representative trace, and dashboards keyed on trace_id to move between metrics, traces, and logs in one click.
productionDeepDive.security: Treat telemetry as potentially sensitive: never put secrets, full tokens, PII, or request bodies into span attributes or log fields; redact or hash where needed. Bound metric label cardinality so user-controlled values can't explode the series count (a DoS and cost risk). Secure the OTLP pipeline (TLS + auth to the collector) and restrict access to trace/log backends, since traces can reveal internal topology and identifiers.

caseStudies.problem: Intermittent checkout slowness that no single service dashboard could explain.
caseStudies.solution: Adopted OpenTelemetry across all services with W3C propagation and trace_id-tagged slog logs, exporting to Tempo and Loki via a collector.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Instrumentation and collector infrastructure added operational overhead and required sampling to control cost.
caseStudies.lessons: Correlated traces plus trace-ID logs turned multi-hour cross-team debugging into a single trace lookup, slashing MTTR.

caseStudies.problem: Alert fatigue from raw error-rate thresholds paging on-call for harmless blips.
caseStudies.solution: Defined per-service SLIs/SLOs from a RED histogram and switched to multi-window multi-burn-rate error-budget alerts, with USE dashboards for resources.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Required upfront work to choose SLIs, set realistic SLOs, and tune burn-rate windows.
caseStudies.lessons: Tying pages to error-budget burn dramatically cut false pages while still catching real incidents fast, and made reliability-vs-velocity tradeoffs explicit.

keyTakeaways: Observability rests on three pillars — metrics (aggregate, for alerting), logs (discrete detail), and traces (the cross-service path of one request) — and their power comes from correlating them with a shared trace ID.
Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry models a request as a tree of spans; you create child spans at meaningful boundaries and export them over OTLP to Jaeger/Tempo.

Trace context propagates via a propagator (W3C traceparent header / gRPC metadata); use otelhttp and gRPC interceptors, set a global propagator, and always pass the request context so the trace stays connected.
Thread the trace ID from context.Context onto every structured (slog/zap) log line so you can pivot from a metric to a trace to the exact logs for one request across all services.
A goroutine or queue is a boundary like an RPC: carry the trace context across it (context.WithoutCancel for background work that outlives the request) or spans become orphaned.
Use RED (Rate/Errors/Duration) for services and USE (Utilization/Saturation/Errors) for resources; turn them into SLIs/SLOs with error budgets and alert on burn rate, not raw thresholds.
